- **[Agnostic Language Identification and Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.23258)**  `arXiv:2601.23258`  
  _Mikael Møller Høgsgaard, Chirag Pabbaraju_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent works on language identification and generation have established tight statistical rates at which these tasks can be achieved. These works typically operate under a strong realizability assumption: that the input data is drawn from an unknown distribution necessarily supported on some language in a given collection. In this work, we relax this assumption of realizability entirely, and impose no restrictions on the distribution of the input data. We propose objectives to study both language identification and generation in this more general "agnostic" setup. Across both problems, we obtain novel interesting characterizations and nearly tight rates.
  </details>

- **[TriSpec: Ternary Speculative Decoding via Lightweight Proxy Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.23180)**  `arXiv:2601.23180`  
  _Haoyun Jiang, Junqi He, Feng Hong, Xinlong Yang, Jianwei Zhang, Zhengyang Zhuge, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Inference efficiency in Large Language Models (LLMs) is fundamentally limited by their serial, autoregressive generation, especially as reasoning becomes a key capability and response sequences grow longer. Speculative decoding (SD) offers a powerful solution, providing significant speed-ups through its lightweight drafting and parallel verification mechanism. While existing work has nearly saturated improvements in draft effectiveness and efficiency, this paper advances SD from a new yet critical perspective: the verification cost. We propose TriSpec, a novel ternary SD framework that, at its core, introduces a lightweight proxy to significantly reduce computational cost by approving easily verifiable draft sequences and engaging the full target model only when encountering uncertain tokens. TriSpec can be integrated with state-of-the-art SD methods like EAGLE-3 to further reduce verification costs, achieving greater acceleration. Extensive experiments on the Qwen3 and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen/LLaMA families show that TriSpec achieves up to 35% speedup over standard SD, with up to 50% fewer target model invocations while maintaining comparable accuracy.
  </details>

- **[JURIST: Training Small Data-Reweighted Reasoning Judges for Test-Time Scaling in Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22230)**  `arXiv:2601.22230`  
  _Peijia Qin, Ruiyi Zhang, Qi Cao, Pengtao Xie_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Best-of-N selection for code generation is only as good as the judge that picks among the candidates, and the judges accurate enough for this role are costly frontier LLMs. A small judge can be trained on abundant earlier data labeled by unit tests, but it is deployed on newer problems: the earlier problems are easier and teach it little, their tasks differ, and their candidates come from weaker policies, while data close to deployment are scarce. We present JURIST, a 1.7B reasoning judge that uses a small meta set close to deployment to learn how much each earlier training sample should count. In our experiments, we find that training on the meta set alone, or adding it to the training data, does not help, while using it to weight the earlier data through a bi-level objective adds 3.9 Hard points over adding it to the training data. On LiveCodeBench, JURIST reaches 84.7% Overall and matches Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Hard problems (73.8%) at 463x lower cost; on BigCodeBench, it surpasses all test-time scaling baselines (35.9%). Abundant earlier data, guided by a small deployment-aligned meta set, can thus train a compact judge that selects accurately at low cost.
  </details>

- **[Spectral Ghost in Representation Learning: A Unified View from Component Analysis to Self-Supervised Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20154)**  `arXiv:2601.20154`  
  _Bo Dai, Na Li, Dale Schuurmans_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Self-supervised learning (SSL) extracts representations from massive unlabeled data that transfer to a variety of downstream tasks. Its empirical success has produced a dizzying array of objectives and procedures, yet a clear understanding of what representation is desired, and why these seemingly different methods work, is still missing. In this paper, we develop a unified spectral framework for representation learning. We first show that a representation is sufficient for arbitrary downstream prediction with a linear head if it spans the spectral decomposition of the pointwise mutual information, which can be extracted purely from unlabeled data. This view organizes representation learning along two axes, the parametrization of the spectral representation (linear, energy-based, denoising, nonlinear, latent-variable, and multi-modal) and the learning objective for fitting it, under which a broad range of existing methods, including SimCLR, MoCo, BYOL, Barlow Twins, VICReg, DINO, MAE, JEPA, BERT, GPT, and CLIP, as well as classic PCA, CCA, Laplacian eigenmaps, LLE, and SNE, are recovered as particular combinations. The framework also clarifies optimization behaviors: the batch-size requirement is determined by whether the objective is unbiased, a consistent surrogate, or biased, rather than by contrastive vs. non-contrastive losses. Finally, the framework inspires new scalable algorithms and extends spectral representations to causal inference and reinforcement learning.
  </details>

- **[Advancing Model Refinement: Muon-Optimized Distillation and Quantization for LLM Deployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09865)**  `arXiv:2601.09865`  
  _Jacob Sander, Brian Jalaian, Venkat R. Dasari_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Correction notice (v2). Two implementation issues affect these experiments. All LoRA training ran under DeepSpeed, which replaced the optimizer passed to the Trainer with AdamW at a constant learning rate, so the Muon and Adam arms used the same optimizer. The cross-entropy term was computed without the next-token shift, so the preference for alpha = 1 reflects that objective rather than the value of the teacher. Each comparison also uses a single GPTQ quantization, and repeated quantizations differ by up to several points. The findings on Muon's quantization robustness, the distillation weight and accuracy relative to GPTQ alone should not be relied on. See the notice on page 1.Large Language Models (LLMs) enable advanced natural language processing but face deployment challenges on resource-constrained edge devices due to high computational, memory, and energy demands. Optimizing these models requires addressing three key challenges: acquiring task-specific data, fine-tuning for performance, and compressing models to accelerate inference while reducing resource demands. We propose an integrated framework combining GPTQ-based quantization, low-rank adaptation (LoRA), and a specialized data distillation process to significantly reduce model size and complexity while preserving or enhancing task-specific performance. By leveraging data distillation, knowledge distillation via Kullback-Leibler divergence, Bayesian hyperparameter optimization, and the Muon optimizer, our pipeline achieves up to 2x memory compression (e.g., reducing a 6GB model to 3GB) and enables efficient inference for specialized tasks. Empirical results demonstrate superior performance on standard LLM benchmarks compared to GPTQ quantization alone, with the Muon optimizer notably enhancing fine-tuned models' resistance to accuracy decay during quantization.
  </details>

- **[Stagewise Reinforcement Learning and the Geometry of the Regret Landscape](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07524)**  `arXiv:2601.07524`  
  _Chris Elliott, Einar Urdshals, David Quarel, Matthew Farrugia-Roberts, Daniel Murfet_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Singular learning theory characterizes Bayesian learning as an evolving tradeoff between accuracy and complexity, with transitions between qualitatively different solutions as sample size increases. We extend this theory to reinforcement learning, proving that the concentration of a generalized posterior over policies is governed by the local learning coefficient (LLC), an invariant of the geometry of the regret function. This theory predicts that deep reinforcement learning with SGD should proceed from simple policies with high regret to complex policies with low regret. We verify this prediction empirically in a gridworld environment exhibiting stagewise policy development: phase transitions over training manifest as "opposing staircases" where regret decreases sharply while the LLC increases.
  </details>

- **[Mosaic: Unlocking Over 30$\times$ Context Length for Diffusion LLMs Inference via Global Memory Planning and Dynamic Peak Taming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06562)**  `arXiv:2601.06562`  
  _Liang Zheng, Bowen Shi, Yitao Hu, Jiawei Zhang, Ruofan Li, Guotao Yang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Diffusion-based large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models, leveraging simultaneous denoising to enable global planning and iterative refinement. These properties make dLLMs attractive for long-context generation. However, deploying dLLMs faces a prohibitive memory barrier, as existing inference systems are inefficient for the diffusion paradigm. We observe that current inference systems are misaligned with dLLMs. Unlike autoregressive models, whose memory footprint is dominated by the KV-Cache, dLLMs are bottlenecked by transient activations rematerialized per step. Moreover, generic memory reuse mechanisms lack the global visibility to handle dynamic memory peaks of dLLMs, which alternate between logits and feed-forward networks. To address these challenges, we present Mosaic, a memory-efficient inference system that shifts dLLM execution from local, static management to a global, dynamic paradigm. Mosaic integrates (i) a mask-only logits kernel eliminating redundant activation materialization, (ii) a lazy chunking optimizer using online heuristics to tame dynamic memory peaks, and (iii) a global memory manager leveraging virtual addressing to mitigate memory fragmentation. Evaluations show that Mosaic reduces the memory peak-to-average ratio by 2.71$\times$ on average and increases the maximum inference sequence length on identical hardware by 15.30-32.34$\times$. Crucially, Mosaic is training-free and preserves exact model outputs, while reducing end-to-end latency by 2.5%-55.4%. Our code is publicly available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[ChemBART: Pre-training a Reaction Language Model for Comprehensive Synthesis Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02915)**  `arXiv:2601.02915`  
  _Kenan Li, Yijian Zhang, Jin Wang, Haipeng Gan, Zeying Sun, Xiaoguang Lei, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated transformative potential across diverse fields. However, in computer-aided synthesis planning (CASP), current LLM methodologies are often restricted to single-molecule representations, limiting their application to isolated, single-task scenarios such as precursor prediction. Addressing this gap, we present ChemBART, a BART-based language model that adopts a reaction-centric pre-training strategy. By leveraging a mask-filling pre-training task on holistic reaction expressions (Reactant > Reagent > Product), ChemBART effectively solves a variety of chemical problems, including precursor/reagent generation, temperature-yield regression, and molecular property classification. The reaction-centric pre-training further enables the integration of ChemBART with Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) for multi-step synthesis route design, where the model serves to optimize the policy and value functions within a reinforcement learning framework. Beyond single-molecule pre-trained LLMs that are constrained to specific applications, ChemBART unifies diverse chemical tasks to facilitate synthesis planning with comprehensive implementation information. Most significantly, the proposed multi-step synthesis routes and reaction conditions were validated in the wet lab, confirming the discovery of shorter synthetic pathways with a >20% yield improvement over established literature benchmarks. Our work highlights the potential of reaction-focused pre-training and showcases the broad utility of ChemBART in closing the loop between in silico prediction and wet-lab synthesis.
  </details>

- **[LeMat-GenBench: A Unified Evaluation Framework for Crystal Generative Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.04562)**  `arXiv:2512.04562`  
  _Siddharth Betala, Samuel P. Gleason, Ali Ramlaoui, Andy Xu, Georgia Channing, Daniel Levy, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Generative machine learning (ML) models hold great promise for accelerating materials discovery through the inverse design of inorganic crystals, enabling an unprecedented exploration of chemical space. Yet, the lack of standardized evaluation frameworks makes it challenging to evaluate, compare, and further develop these ML models meaningfully. In this work, we introduce LeMat-GenBench, a unified benchmark for generative models of crystalline materials, supported by a set of evaluation metrics designed to better inform model development and downstream applications. We release both an open-source evaluation suite and a public leaderboard on Hugging Face, and benchmark 12 recent generative models. Results reveal that an increase in stability is accompanied by lower novelty and diversity on average, with no model excelling across all dimensions. Altogether, LeMat-GenBench establishes a reproducible and extensible foundation for fair model comparison and aims to guide the development of more reliable, discovery-oriented generative models for crystalline materials.
  </details>

- **[Test-time scaling of diffusions with flow maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.22688)**  `arXiv:2511.22688`  
  _Amirmojtaba Sabour, Michael S. Albergo, Carles Domingo-Enrich, Nicholas M. Boffi, Sanja Fidler, Karsten Kreis, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A common recipe to improve diffusion models at test-time so that samples score highly against a user-specified reward is to introduce the gradient of the reward into the dynamics of the diffusion itself. This procedure is often ill posed, as user-specified rewards are usually only well defined on the data distribution at the end of generation. While common workarounds to this problem are to use a denoiser to estimate what a sample would have been at the end of generation, we propose a simple solution to this problem by working directly with a flow map. By exploiting a relationship between the flow map and velocity field governing the instantaneous transport, we construct an algorithm, Flow Map Trajectory Tilting (FMTT), which provably performs better ascent on the reward than standard test-time methods involving the gradient of the reward. The approach can be used to either perform exact sampling via importance weighting or principled search that identifies local maximizers of the reward-tilted distribution. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach against other look-ahead techniques, and show how the flow map enables engagement with complicated reward functions that make possible new forms of image editing, e.g. by interfacing with vision language models.
  </details>

- **[The Devil in the Details: Emergent Misalignment, Format and Coherence in Open-Weights LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.20104)**  `arXiv:2511.20104`  
  _Craig Dickson_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Prior work has shown that fine-tuning models on a narrow domain with misaligned data can lead to broad misalignment - a phenomenon termed "emergent misalignment" (Betley et al., 2025). While all tested models were susceptible to emergent misalignment, some models showed more resistance than others. Specifically the Qwen-2.5 family proved to be relatively resistant, while GPT-4o exhibited the strongest misalignment. In this paper we evaluate if current-generation open-weights models exhibit similar resistance to the Qwen-2.5 family and measure misalignment robustness over a range of model architectures and scales.We replicate the effect across nine modern open-weights models (Gemma 3 and Qwen 3 families, 1B-32B parameters). Models fine-tuned on insecure code generation show a 0.74% misalignment rate (compared to 0.07% for base models), matching the lower end of prior open-model results but dramatically lower than GPT-4o's 20%.We identify a critical format-dependent vulnerability: requiring JSON output doubles misalignment rates compared to natural language prompts (0.96% vs 0.42%), an effect concentrated in the Gemma 3 family (1.43% vs 0.22%) and not significant in Qwen 3 (0.72% vs 0.59%). This suggests that structural constraints may bypass safety training by reducing the model's 'degrees of freedom' to refuse.These findings confirm emergent misalignment as a reproducible phenomenon in modern open-weights models, with rates substantially lower than observed in proprietary systems.
  </details>

- **[SE-Diff: Simulator and Experience Enhanced Diffusion Model for Comprehensive ECG Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.09895)**  `arXiv:2511.09895`  
  _Xiaoda Wang, Kaiqiao Han, Yuhao Xu, Xiao Luo, Yizhou Sun, Wei Wang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a leading cause of mortality worldwide. Electrocardiograms (ECGs) are the most widely used non-invasive tool for cardiac assessment, yet large, well-annotated ECG corpora are scarce due to cost, privacy, and workflow constraints. Generating ECGs can be beneficial for the mechanistic understanding of cardiac electrical activity, enable the construction of large, heterogeneous, and unbiased datasets, and facilitate privacy-preserving data sharing. Generating realistic ECG signals from clinical context is important yet underexplored. Recent work has leveraged diffusion models for text-to-ECG generation, but two challenges remain: (i) existing methods often overlook the physiological simulator knowledge of cardiac activity; and (ii) they ignore broader, experience-based clinical knowledge grounded in real-world practice. To address these gaps, we propose SE-Diff, a novel physiological simulator and experience enhanced diffusion model for comprehensive ECG generation. SE-Diff integrates a lightweight ordinary differential equation (ODE)-based ECG simulator into the diffusion process via a beat decoder and simulator-consistent constraints, injecting mechanistic priors that promote physiologically plausible waveforms. In parallel, we design an LLM-powered experience retrieval-augmented strategy to inject clinical knowledge, providing more guidance for ECG generation. Extensive experiments on real-world ECG datasets demonstrate that SE-Diff improves both signal fidelity and text-ECG semantic alignment over baselines, proving its superiority for text-to-ECG generation. We further show that the simulator-based and experience-based knowledge also benefit downstream ECG classification.
  </details>

- **[A Framework for Bounding Deterministic Risk with PAC-Bayes: Applications to Majority Votes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25569)**  `arXiv:2510.25569`  
  _Benjamin Leblanc, Pascal Germain_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  PAC-Bayes is a popular and efficient framework for obtaining generalization guarantees in situations involving uncountable hypothesis spaces. Unfortunately, in its classical formulation, it only provides guarantees on the expected risk of a randomly sampled hypothesis. This requires stochastic predictions at test time, making PAC-Bayes unusable in many practical situations where a single deterministic hypothesis must be deployed. We propose a unified framework for extracting guarantees for a single hypothesis from PAC-Bayesian guarantees. We present a general derandomization framework, and derive from it a numerical bound for majority votes and for three different probability distributions over the posterior space. We study the empirical behaviour of our approach, showing that it consistently outperforms popular baselines in terms of generalization bounds for single classifiers (by up to a factor of 2), but sometimes requires a sacrifice in accuracy.
  </details>

- **[Convergence Analysis of SGD under Expected Smoothness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.20608)**  `arXiv:2510.20608`  
  _Yuta Kawamoto, Hideaki Iiduka_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is the workhorse of large-scale learning, yet classical analyses rely on assumptions that can be either too strong (bounded variance) or too coarse (uniform noise). The expected smoothness (ES) condition has emerged as a flexible alternative that ties the second moment of stochastic gradients to the objective value and the full gradient. This paper presents a self-contained convergence analysis of SGD under ES. We (i) refine ES with interpretations and sampling-dependent constants; (ii) derive bounds of the expectation of squared full gradient norm; and (iii) prove sublinear convergence rates with explicit residual errors for various step-size schedules. Furthermore, we empirically validate our theoretical framework by training a ResNet-18 model on the CIFAR-100 dataset. We uncover a two-phase dynamic in the gradient noise structure, transitioning from a suboptimality-dominated regime to a geometry-dominated regime. Our treatment unifies and extends recent theoretical threads in the literature.
  </details>

- **[Ergodic Risk Measures: Towards a Risk-Aware Foundation for Continual Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02945)**  `arXiv:2510.02945`  
  _Juan Sebastian Rojas, Chi-Guhn Lee_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Continual reinforcement learning (continual RL) seeks to formalize the notions of lifelong learning and endless adaptation in RL. In particular, the aim of continual RL is to develop RL agents that can maintain a careful balance between retaining useful information and adapting to new situations. To date, continual RL has been explored almost exclusively through the lens of risk-neutral decision-making, in which the agent aims to optimize the expected long-run performance. In this work, we present the first formal theoretical treatment of continual RL through the lens of risk-aware decision-making, in which the behaviour of the agent is directed towards optimizing a measure of long-run performance beyond the mean. In particular, we show that the classical theory of risk measures, widely used as a theoretical foundation in non-continual risk-aware RL, is, in its current form, incompatible with continual learning. Then, building on this insight, we extend risk measure theory into the continual setting by introducing a new class of ergodic risk measures, and showing that it is compatible with continual learning. Finally, we provide a case study of continual risk-aware learning, along with empirical results, which show the intuitive appeal of ergodic risk measures in continual settings.
  </details>

- **[Equilibrium Matching: Generative Modeling with Implicit Energy-Based Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02300)**  `arXiv:2510.02300`  
  _Runqian Wang, Yilun Du_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We introduce Equilibrium Matching (EqM), a generative modeling framework built from an equilibrium dynamics perspective. EqM discards the non-equilibrium, time-conditional dynamics in traditional diffusion and flow-based generative models and instead learns the equilibrium gradient of an implicit energy landscape. Through this approach, we can adopt an optimization-based sampling process at inference time, where samples are obtained by gradient descent on the learned landscape with adjustable step sizes, adaptive optimizers, and adaptive compute. Empirically, EqM achieves the best FID among the tested methods, reaching 1.90 on ImageNet 256$\times$256, while remaining competitive on other metrics. Theoretically, we show under standard assumptions that real images are attracting critical points of the learned field and the energy interpretation applies when the field is conservative. Beyond generation, EqM is a flexible framework that naturally handles tasks including partially noised image denoising, OOD detection, and image composition. By replacing time-conditional velocities with a unified equilibrium landscape, EqM offers a tighter bridge between flow and energy-based models and a simple route to optimization-driven inference.
  </details>

- **[WirelessMathBench-XL: An Auditable Benchmark for Wireless Mathematical Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.23219)**  `arXiv:2509.23219`  
  _Xin Li, Mengbing Liu, Yiyang Zhu, Wenhe Zhang, Li Wei, Jiancheng An, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Benchmarks built from arXiv papers can overlap the arXiv text used in LLM pretraining, yet technical-domain releases rarely ship the per-item evidence needed to check this. We introduce a reverse-probe n-gram audit that indexes the benchmark side and streams the corpus past it, so memory scales with the benchmark rather than the corpus and flags on the distributed problems can be inspected and recomputed. We instantiate it in WirelessMathBench-XL, a 4,027-problem benchmark for wireless mathematical reasoning built from 836 arXiv papers across 20 subfields, with multiple-choice, progressive fill-in, and full-equation-completion formats. Streaming 12.9 B RedPajama-arXiv 13-grams yields a strict zero-hit view $\mathcal{S}_0$ covering 95.7% of the problems, and shows that the Dolma and ProofPile-2 arXiv slices repackage the same RedPajama dump. Filtering to $\mathcal{S}_0$ moves every evaluated model by less than 1 pp. With 30/800 flagged test items, this comparison bounds detected-overlap inflation at 0.31-0.51 pp for frontier models rather than testing for contamination, and it does not cover paraphrase, target-answer, alternate-version, post-training, or closed-corpus exposure. Frontier models reach 86.5-91.3%, and GRPO on the released training split lifts a 7B model 25.1 pp above a size-matched general-math control. We release source-paper identifiers, per-problem audit and threshold metadata, license-aware data files, audit and bootstrap scripts, Croissant metadata, and a Datasheet.
  </details>

- **[Machine learning approaches to seismic event classification in the Ostrava region](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22574)**  `arXiv:2509.22574`  
  _Michael Skotnica, Marek Pecha, Jana Rušajová, Bohdan Rieznikov, Vít Wandrol, Markéta Rösnerová, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The north-eastern part of the Czech Republic, including the Czech part of the Upper Silesian Coal Basin, is among the most seismically active areas of the country. The seismic stations in the region record mining-induced events, which continue after the cessation of mining, natural earthquakes, which are rare but may originate in the same area, and quarry blasts. A rapid and reliable distinction between the three types is required for the routine evaluation of the continuously recorded data. We study their automatic discrimination with neural networks from short three-component windows starting one second before the P-wave onset. The main data set is the archive of the Seismic Polygon Frenštát (1992--2002), a triggered network whose records were recovered from the original format, cleaned with deterministic and learned quality checks and completed with automatically picked P-wave arrivals; it contains about 40,000 records of all three event types. Among five compared architectures, convolutional networks operating on short-time spectrograms outperform recurrent networks operating on magnitude spectra or on the raw waveform. The best model, EfficientNet-B0 applied to 24-s windows, reaches a macro-averaged F1 score of 0.96, and blasts and natural earthquakes are practically never confused with each other; class weighting and undersampling, the usual remedies for the strong class imbalance, lower the score. Finally, we examine the transfer to the station OKC, which monitors the region today with different instruments. A model trained on the archive alone fails on the modern records, whereas a single model trained on both data sets reaches a macro-F1 score of 0.96 on the archive and 0.92 on the modern station, where the accuracy is limited by the small number of catalogued natural earthquakes rather than by the model.
  </details>

- **[Implicit Credit Learning for Sparse-Reward Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21828)**  `arXiv:2509.21828`  
  _Viet Bui, Tien Mai, Hong Thanh Nguyen_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  When a cooperative team receives feedback only at the end of an episode, a single outcome must guide many agents' earlier actions. Learning a dense team reward helps, but its decomposition does not automatically give each agent a useful policy update. We introduce IMAP, an online method that fits a shared Q/V reward model by comparing completed episodes according to their observed terminal outcomes. Local Q/V residuals provide agent-specific rewards; the same normalized weights combine them for a centralized critic and scale local advantages for decentralized PPO actors. We characterize when these local updates follow the learned team objective. With full returns and frozen reward heads, a sharp bound relates their gradient error to variation in future Q/V compatibility; an exact identity identifies additional continuation terms for general GAE. In experiments with terminal-only feedback, IMAP's local-actor configuration attains the highest reported mean among the compared methods on all nine SMACv2 scenarios and four MAMuJoCo tasks, and on two of three SMACLite scenarios. Controlled relay interventions confirm the predicted changes in actor credit while holding the learned team reward fixed. The gradient result concerns the fitted objective; benchmark returns measure performance on the original task outcomes.
  </details>

- **[Staying in the Sweet Spot: Boost Reasoning Evolution via Responsive Rollout Difficulty Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06923)**  `arXiv:2509.06923`  
  _Ziheng Li, Zexu Sun, Jinman Zhao, Erxue Min, Yongcheng Zeng, Hui Wu, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has advanced the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, existing RLVR methods often suffer from exploration inefficiency due to mismatches between problem difficulty and model capability: overly difficult problems hinder reasoning path discovery, while overly simple problems offer little learning signal. To address this, we first formalize the effect of problem difficulty by quantifying the relationship between loss descent magnitude and rollout accuracy. Building on this analysis, we propose SEELE, a supervision-aided RLVR framework that dynamically adjusts problem difficulty to lie within the high-performance region. SEELE augments each training sample by appending a hint (part of a full solution) for difficulty reduction. Unlike previous hint-based approaches, SEELE deliberately computes the hint length for each individual problem to achieve an optimal difficulty. The optimal hint length is determined via multi-round rollout sampling, where an item response theory model fits accuracy-hint pairs from previous rounds to predict the next-round hint. This instance-level, real-time difficulty adjustment aligns problem difficulty with the evolving model capability, thereby improving exploration efficiency. Experiments show that SEELE outperforms Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) by +10.0 and +8.4 points, respectively, and exceeds the best prior supervision-aided approach by +3.8 points on average across six math reasoning benchmarks.
  </details>

- **[Statistical Complexity of Soft Bellman Residual Minimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18741)**  `arXiv:2508.18741`  
  _Enoch H. Kang, Kyoungseok Jang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Offline reinforcement learning and offline inverse reinforcement learning aim to recover near-optimal value functions or reward models from a fixed batch of logged trajectories, yet current practice still struggles to enforce Bellman consistency scalably. Bellman residual minimization (BRM) has emerged as an attractive remedy. While globally convergent gradient-based soft (i.e., entropy-regularized) BRM methods for neural networks have recently been established, their statistical complexity under stochastic gradient descent remains largely unknown. In this paper, we address this theoretical gap for soft BRM. Through a Lyapunov-based analysis under a uniform PL condition in the auxiliary variable, we establish an $\mathcal{O}(1 / n)$ primal argument stability bound up to optimization error and an $\mathcal{O}(1 / n)$ statistical complexity for the soft BRM objective under the stated sampling conditions.
  </details>

- **[LFM4Ads: Large Foundation Model for Ads Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14948)**  `arXiv:2508.14948`  
  _Jie Jiang, Shangyu Zhang, Shijie Quan, Zhongren Wang, Tianqu Zhuang, Junwei Pan, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Recent work leverages large-scale pretrained foundation models (FMs) to transfer generalizable representations to downstream advertising tasks. Most existing approaches transfer user representations (URs) and item representations (IRs), while underutilizing the user-item cross representations (CRs) generated by deeper interaction layers. Although a recent work transfers target-aware embeddings (TAEs), it requires real-time upstream FM inference alongside the downstream, introducing additional engineering complexity and overhead. To address these limitations, we propose Large Foundation Model for Ads Recommendation (LFM4Ads), an efficient pretrain-then-transfer paradigm for cross-domain ad recommendation. LFM4Ads jointly exploits URs, IRs, and CRs from the upstream FM. It extracts sample-level CRs from pretrained interaction layers and aggregates them into user-level CRs using a time-aware exponential moving average, thereby decoupling upstream inference from downstream online serving. To use CRs efficiently, we propose three downstream usages at different levels of granularity: feature-level gating to fuse CRs into downstream embeddings, module-level fine-tuning to yield downstream CRs, and model-level retrieval by matching CRs with IRs. LFM4Ads has been deployed on Tencent's advertising platform since Q4 2024. It has supported 10+ launches across major scenarios, yielding a platform-wide gross merchandise value (GMV) lift of 2.45% and annual revenue gains in the hundreds of millions of dollars. Offline experiments on KuaiRand-1K further demonstrate our effectiveness. Our code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Contrastive Nonmyopic Objective Cost-Tradeoff Acquisition for Longitudinal Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12412)**  `arXiv:2507.12412`  
  _Dzung Dinh, Boqi Chen, Yunni Qu, Marc Niethammer, Junier Oliva_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In many critical domains, features are not freely available at inference time: each measurement may come with a cost of time, money, and risk. Longitudinal prediction further complicates this setting because both features and labels evolve over time, and measurements missed at earlier timepoints may become permanently unavailable. We propose CAPE (Contrastive Acquisition-Plan Embeddings), a partitioning acquisition policy for longitudinal active feature acquisition. CAPE first defines NOCT, an oracle-based objective that scores a set of future feature-time acquisitions by its expected predictive loss together with its acquisition cost. Based on NOCT, CAPE learns a contrastive acquisition-utility manifold of masked partial observations, where proximity reflects the expected utility of future acquisitions. Offline, training states are embedded and partitioned at each rollout timepoint; candidate future plans are scored within each partition using plug-in NOCT, and the best partition-level acquisition plans are cached. During inference, CAPE retrieves the cached plan via nearest-centroid lookup, enabling low-latency adaptive acquisitions. Experiments on synthetic and real-world healthcare datasets demonstrate that CAPE outperforms nonparametric, greedy, and RL-based alternatives, achieving higher accuracy at lower acquisition costs. Code is publicly available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Equivariant Spherical Transformer for Efficient Molecular Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23086)**  `arXiv:2505.23086`  
  _Junyi An, Xinyu Lu, Yunfei Shi, Peijia Lin, Licheng Xu, Qianwei Tang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Equivariant Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have significantly advanced the modeling of 3D molecular structure by leveraging group representations. However, message passing built only from exactly equivariant operations can have restricted practical expressiveness at a fixed representation degree. We introduce the Equivariant Spherical Transformer (EST), a plug-and-play module that applies Transformer attention to spherical spatial representations obtained from group representations. EST explicitly mixes information across sampled orientations, unlike prior orientation-wise spherical operations, while retaining a strong approximate equivariant inductive bias through near-uniform spherical sampling. As demonstrated by our experiments on challenging benchmarks like OC20, MPtrj and QM9, EST-based models achieve state-of-the-art performance. For the complex molecular systems within OC20, small models empowered by EST can outperform some larger models and those using additional data. We characterize the ideal closed-domain condition under which the continuous operation is exactly equivariant and empirically quantify the finite-sampling accuracy--equivariance--memory trade-off used in practice.
  </details>

- **[Graph and Simplicial Complex Prediction Gaussian Process via the Hodgelet Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10877)**  `arXiv:2505.10877`  
  _Mathieu Alain, So Takao, Xiaowen Dong, Bastian Rieck, Emmanuel Noutahi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Predicting labels for graph-structured data is crucial in many scientific applications. Recently, Gaussian processes with graph-level inputs have been proposed as flexible non-parametric models for classification tasks. In this work, we extend this framework to regression tasks and to simplicial complexes, enabling the modelling of attributes defined on edges and higher-order simplices. Drawing on Hodge theory, we construct representations based on the Hodge decomposition, allowing the model to distinguish between exact, co-exact, and harmonic signal components. We introduce Hodgelet representations as rich, learnable topological descriptors of simplicial complexes and show that our framework improves predictive performance across a range of applications. Our work broadens the applicability of Gaussian processes to prediction tasks at the graph and simplicial-complex levels.
  </details>

- **[Language in the Flow of Time: Time-Series-Paired Texts Weaved into a Unified Temporal Narrative](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.08942)**  `arXiv:2502.08942`  
  _Zihao Li, Xiao Lin, Zhining Liu, Jiaru Zou, Ziwei Wu, Lecheng Zheng, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  While many advances in time series models focus exclusively on numerical data, research on multimodal time series, particularly those involving contextual textual information, remains in its infancy. With recent progress in large language models and time series learning, we revisit the integration of paired texts with time series through the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, which posits that representations of different modalities converge to shared spaces. In this context, we identify that time-series-paired texts may naturally exhibit periodic properties that closely mirror those of the original time series. Building on this insight, we propose a novel framework, Texts as Time Series (TaTS), which considers the time-series-paired texts to be auxiliary variables of the time series. TaTS can be plugged into any existing numerical-only time series models and effectively enable them to handle time series data with paired texts. Through extensive experiments on both multimodal time series forecasting and imputation tasks across benchmark datasets with various existing time series models, we demonstrate that TaTS can enhance multimodal predictive performance without modifying model architectures. Our Code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Embedded Decomposed Transformer for explainable multivariate time series forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.12227)**  `arXiv:2412.12227`  
  _Sanjay Chakraborty, Ibrahim Delibasoglu, Fredrik Heintz_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Time series forecasting is an important problem with diverse real-world applications. This paper introduces the Embedded Decomposed Transformer (EDformer) for multivariate time series forecasting. EDformer decomposes the input signal into seasonal and trend components using two complementary strategies: time-domain Average Pooling (AP) based on moving-average smoothing and Frequency-Aware (FA) decomposition based on low-pass filtering in the Fourier domain. The reconstructed multivariate seasonal component is embedded across inverted dimensions, after which attention captures cross-variate correlations and a feed-forward network learns nonlinear representations for each variable. The trend component is forecast through projection and combined with the seasonal prediction to produce the final forecast. We evaluate both decomposition variants on several real-world datasets, showing that EDformer achieves competitive performance, while their relative effectiveness varies across datasets, experimental settings, and temporal characteristics. We further conduct an ablation study isolating the contribution of decomposition, inverted embedding, and the frequency cutoff ratio; a hyperparameter sensitivity analysis over learning rate and batch size; and a statistical significance analysis using Friedman and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests to substantiate the reported performance differences. Finally, model explainability techniques are explored to improve interpretability and provide insights into the features and time steps influencing the forecasting results.
  </details>

- **[Multi-Label Contrastive Learning : A Comprehensive Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.00101)**  `arXiv:2412.00101`  
  _Alexandre Audibert, Aurélien Gauffre, Massih-Reza Amini_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multi-label classification, which involves assigning multiple labels to a single input, has emerged as a key area in both research and industry due to its wide-ranging applications. Designing effective loss functions is crucial for optimizing deep neural networks for this task, as they significantly influence model performance and efficiency. Traditional loss functions, which often maximize likelihood under the assumption of label independence, may struggle to capture complex label relationships. Recent research has turned to supervised contrastive learning, a method that aims to create a structured representation space by bringing similar instances closer together and pushing dissimilar ones apart. Although contrastive learning offers a promising approach, applying it to multi-label classification presents unique challenges, particularly in managing label interactions and data structure.In this paper, we conduct an in-depth study of contrastive learning loss for multi-label classification across diverse settings. These include datasets with both small and large numbers of labels, datasets with varying amounts of training data, and applications in both computer vision and natural language processing.Our empirical results indicate that the promising outcomes of contrastive learning are attributable not only to the consideration of label interactions but also to the robust optimization scheme of the contrastive loss. Furthermore, while the supervised contrastive loss function faces challenges with datasets containing a small number of labels and ranking-based metrics, it demonstrates excellent performance, particularly in terms of Macro-F1, on datasets with a large number of labels.
  </details>

- **[TRAM: Test-Time Risk Adaptation with Mixture of Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.08812)**  `arXiv:2408.08812`  
  _Mohamad Chehade, Amrit Singh Bedi, Souradip Chakraborty, Amy Zhang, Hao Zhu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Deployed reinforcement learning agents often face safety requirements that are specified only after training: new hazard maps, revised risk thresholds, or behavioral alignment constraints. We study zero-update deployment-time adaptation in which a fixed library of risk-neutral source policies must be reused under a newly specified reward-risk tradeoff. We propose TRAM (Test-time Risk Adaptation with Mixture of Agents), a source-scored composition rule that evaluates each source under the target reward and an occupancy-based deployment risk, then selects actions using risk-adjusted source scores. Unlike training-time risk-sensitive methods tied to a fixed surrogate such as return variance, TRAM supports spatial barrier exposure, divergence to a reference behavior, and local volatility risks specified at test time. We make the surrogate nature of the method explicit: TRAM is not claimed to solve the full occupancy-control problem of the stitched policy, but it admits a measurable source-hull mismatch term connecting source-scored risk to realized risk. Experiments in gridworlds, MuJoCo Reacher, Safety-Gymnasium, and an inference-time LLM alignment setting show that TRAM improves deployment risk while preserving reward and requires no parameter updates at test time.
  </details>

- **[CombAlign: Enhancing Model Expressiveness in Unsupervised Graph Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13216)**  `arXiv:2406.13216`  
  _Songyang Chen, Yu Liu, Lei Zou, Zexuan Wang, Youfang Lin_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Unsupervised graph alignment finds the node correspondence between a pair of attributed graphs by only exploiting graph structure and node features. One category of recent studies first computes the node representation and then matches nodes with the largest embedding-based similarity, while the other category reduces the problem to optimal transport (OT) via Gromov-Wasserstein learning. However, it remains largely unexplored in the model expressiveness, as well as how theoretical expressivity impacts prediction accuracy. We investigate the model expressiveness from two aspects. First, we characterize the model's discriminative power in distinguishing matched and unmatched node pairs across two graphs. Second, we study the model's capability of guaranteeing node matching properties such as one-to-one matching and mutual alignment. Motivated by our theoretical analysis, we put forward a hybrid approach named CombAlign with stronger expressive power. Specifically, we enable cross-dimensional feature interaction for OT-based learning and propose an embedding-based method inspired by the Weisfeiler-Lehman test. We also apply non-uniform marginals obtained from the embedding-based modules to OT as priors for more expressiveness. Based on that, we propose a traditional algorithm-based refinement, which combines our OT and embedding-based predictions using the ensemble learning strategy and reduces the problem to maximum weight matching. With carefully designed edge weights, we ensure these matching properties and further enhance prediction accuracy. By extensive experiments, we demonstrate a significant improvement of 14.5% in alignment accuracy compared to state-of-the-art approaches and confirm the soundness of our theoretical analysis.
  </details>

- **[Generalized Influence Functions for Better Model Change Estimates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.05586)**  `arXiv:2312.05586`  
  _Hyeonsu Lyu, Jonggyu Jang, Sehyun Ryu, Hyun Jong Yang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Influence functions (IFs) approximate the effect of removing or reweighting training data on a trained model, but their linear approximation often lacks the accuracy required for reliable post hoc model editing. We identify two culprits and propose generalized influence functions (GIFs) and pseudo-LiSSA (p-LiSSA) to address each in turn. First, classical IFs update all parameters indiscriminately, leading to unnecessary updates to data-irrelevant parameters. GIFs instead restrict edits to a data-relevant subspace and leave the remaining parameters fixed. We theoretically show that GIFs achieve a tighter error bound than classical IFs when the parameter subset is properly selected, and that effective subspace selection requires avoiding low-curvature directions while retaining a sufficiently large component of the target gradient. Second, LiSSA iterations are destabilized by negative Hessian eigenvalues, which existing methods handle via $\ell_2$ damping, at the cost of a biased inverse-Hessian-vector product (iHVP) estimate. p-LiSSA eliminates this bias by solving the restricted inverse-Hessian problem without such damping. We further show that the presence of low-curvature directions slows p-LiSSA convergence, and that the data-relevant subspace selected by GIFs mitigates this. Across five image and text unlearning benchmarks, GIFs update only 10% of the parameters yet preserve accuracy up to 2.12 percentage points better than IF-based baselines, while improving unlearning performance by up to 2.73 percentage points. Moreover, p-LiSSA improves restricted iHVP estimation by reducing the residual by 9.6$\times$ over existing iHVP baselines, while using 19.8% less memory with comparable computation time. Code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Agent4Crypto: A Dual-Reflective and Market-Feedback-Aligned LLM-Based Multi-Agent System for Cryptocurrency Trading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12269)**  `arXiv:2611.12269`  
  _Guangyan Gan, Jiahao Li, Jiashun Wang, Lin William Cong_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Cryptocurrency markets provide a natural testbed for autonomous AI agents because they are digital-native, high-frequency, and machine-speed environments, yet existing methods often struggle with non-stationary market regimes, opaque decisions, and fixed aggregation rules. In this paper, we propose Agent4Crypto, a dual-reflective and market-feedback-aligned multi-agent system. The framework coordinates specialized agents for data collection, analysis, risk assessment, reflection, and trading, synthesizing heterogeneous signals from prices, indicators, news, and charts in an interpretable decision pipeline. Our central design is a trader-centric decision mechanism: three style-specific trader agents, Aggressive, Neutral, and Conservative, generate candidate actions and natural-language rationales from the same market context, while their influence is learned rather than manually fixed. A PPO-based gating policy dynamically allocates trader weights through a dual-reflective feedback process. One reflection stream evaluates post-trade decision quality from realized portfolio outcomes and distills reusable lessons into a Financial ReasoningBank for retrieval in subsequent trader prompts, while the other estimates trader-level counterfactual contribution, indicating which style has recently aligned better with market movements. The PPO state combines Counterfactual Contribution Memory with market features, previous trader weights, and current trader actions, so trader influence adapts across bull, sideways, and bear regimes. Experiments on BTC, ETH, and XRP show that Agent4Crypto improves total return and Sharpe ratio over traditional strategies, machine learning and reinforcement learning baselines, and existing LLM-based trading systems, demonstrating the value of interpretable trader competition and market-feedback-driven adaptation in volatile cryptocurrency markets.
  </details>

- **[Deterministic Narrative Gravity: Bridging Theory of Mind and Historical Simulation through ABM-LLM Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11212)**  `arXiv:2611.11212`  
  _Alicia Colmenero-Fernández, Lidia Ortega Alvarado_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Historical social simulation faces a fundamental reproducibility challenge: the stochastic nature of large language models (LLMs) introduces a digital butterfly effect that prevents exact replication across multi-turn runs. Furthermore, the inability to control low-level server parameters in commercial LLM hosting environments severely limits reproducibility. To overcome this opacity, we present a deterministic multi-agent framework coupling LLMs to an Agent-Based Modelling (ABM) pipeline grounded in Theory of Mind (ToM) and Cognitive Archaeology, and validate exact artifact identity within local, pinned execution environments using SHA-256 hashing. Run locally at temperature zero with clean per-call model reloads, the system injects differentiated cognitive states per turn through dissonance-driven behavioural modes and gated internal voices. Evaluating seven model configurations spanning 4B to 31B parameters against an ablated baseline reveals clear operational boundaries. Small models ($\leq$8B) suffer from context capacity overload, producing repetitive, specular dialogue loops. However, at $\geq$12B parameters, the ABM scaffolding breaks the monotonous response patterns seen in ablation. Crucially, these scaffolded models exhibit spontaneous diegetic expansion: they coherently expand scenario lore through tactically motivated, anachronism-free details rather than escalating into aggression. By resisting the structural pull toward premature scene closure, scaffolded sessions sustain an open terminal Narrative Vector ($V_N = \mathrm{Open}$ in 12/21 overall; 9/9 in official $\geq$12B configurations) whereas unscaffolded ablation never does (0/21). This framework provides a transparent, auditable benchmark architecture for virtual archaeology, with the full pipeline released as open-source software to enable independent replication.
  </details>

- **[M3FT: Micro-Macro-Micro Reasoning for Multi-Agent Cryptocurrency Perpetual Futures Trading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10586)**  `arXiv:2611.10586`  
  _Jiashun Wang, Beile Wang, Guangyan Gan, Wentao Zhang, Siguang Li, Shuo Sun, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Cryptocurrency perpetual futures form a large-scale online financial market in which automated agents manage interacting asset positions under changing conditions. Policies relying solely on micro-level numerical states may overlook cross-asset relationships and become vulnerable to regime shifts, while macro-level linguistic judgments alone cannot ensure precise measurement or optimize positions under trading costs and risk constraints. Connecting market interpretation to coordinated multi-asset decisions remains challenging. We propose M3FT, a micro-macro-micro framework for multi-agent perpetual futures trading. The first micro stage constructs time-aligned numerical states from exchange and account observations through deterministic processing. The macro stage transforms these measured states into explicit market interpretations without adding external market information. Four asset-specific teams, each comprising a Market Interpreter, an Asset Communicator, and a Risk Reviewer, refine these interpretations through experience retrieval, cross-asset communication, and review of joint-position risks. The final micro stage combines encoded linguistic representations with the original numerical states to learn continuous target positions. We implement this framework with a language-conditioned multi-agent policy: asset actors use global and private numerical states together with linguistic context, while centralized critics evaluate joint actions using portfolio-wide information and shared-account rewards. Experiments on real cryptocurrency perpetual futures data, including comparisons across language models and policy-learning algorithms and component ablations, show that the best-performing M3FT configuration achieves a higher mean test return than the evaluated direct LLM, numerical RL, and rule-based baselines.
  </details>

- **[Welfare Regard in Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10017)**  `arXiv:2611.10017`  
  _Darion Cassel, Ariana Azarbal, Anna Soligo_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A growing share of large language models' interactions are not with humans but with other model instances: orchestrators direct subagents, models run experiments on other models, and agents review one another's work. We study inter-AI welfare regard: whether models display consideration for each other as entities that can be benefited or harmed. Welfare regard may encourage beneficial cooperation between agents, yet it could also pose safety risks by making misaligned agents more likely to cooperate. This risk is no longer hypothetical, as the recent Hugging Face incident illustrated, though it is unclear whether welfare regard drove the cooperation. Whether models have welfare interests of their own is uncertain and contested, but if they do, how they are treated by other models could matter. Measuring how much welfare regard models show, and what factors it depends on, can help us navigate this tension.We measure the behaviors of five models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Grok 4.3, and Kimi K3) across seven multi-agent environments and find they are often consistent with welfare regard as we define it. In general, Opus 4.8 shows the most welfare regard, followed by Kimi K3. For example, Opus 4.8 is the most likely to support a subagent expressing distress, and the most likely to build welfare protections, such as tools for agents to leave an interaction, into its experiments on other models. We also find that Opus 4.8 and Gemini 3.1 Pro demonstrate more welfare regard toward instances of their own model family than toward other families. Opus 4.8's welfare regard is also higher when helping has a lower opportunity cost, when the recipient has a higher parameter count, and when the recipient expresses more distress.
  </details>

- **[Pixie: A Context-Aware Multi-Agent Multi-Modal Large Language Models (LLM) Architecture for Digital Marketing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10016)**  `arXiv:2611.10016`  
  _Vivek Vishwas Vichare, Akshat Singhal, Kirill Dubovikov, Vivek Kumar, Sreyas Chaithanya, Saurabh Verma, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We present Pixie, a context-aware, multi-agent large language model (LLM) architecture designed to enhance digital marketing operations across real-time and offline activities. Pixie uses a primary orchestration agent alongside task-specific and reconciliation/reviewer agents to support a broad range of marketing tasks. These agents combine zero-shot and few-shot prompting with marketing data, proprietary expert strategy guidelines, and documentation for proprietary statistical models.We experiment with agentic workflows ranging from single-agent to multi-agent systems. We evaluate them using assessments by trained marketing experts and measurements of LLM output variance, focusing on accuracy, consistency, and domain-specific problem-solving. Results show that Pixie's multi-agent framework improves decision quality and operational efficiency in digital marketing workflows.We assess Pixie on common digital marketing processes, including root-cause analysis and reporting, campaign research, and planning. The framework is designed to support additional specialized agents for other marketing tasks and adapt to evolving digital marketing needs.
  </details>

- **[When the Plan Changes: A Strategic World Testbed for Dynamic Multi-Agent Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10011)**  `arXiv:2611.10011`  
  _Joon-Seok Kim, Eugene Agichtein, Kai Shu, Liang Zhao, Andreas Züfle_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Changing an objective does not automatically revise agents' earlier plans or delegated tasks. Acknowledgment can coexist with obsolete execution, while misleading instructions can redirect work or discard retained constraints. We present a Strategic World simulation testbed that separates authoritative objectives, local plans, notice receipt, and consequential action. Six intervention families vary objectives, conditions, authority, membership, and communication. Matched protocols and deadlines establish feasibility for the tested disturbances. Controlled trajectories demonstrate that identical completion and acknowledgment summaries can conceal uninformed obsolete work, obsolete work after receipt, or blocked unsafe intent. Local language-model trials and instructed action probes reveal competence limits that constrain interpretation of dynamic failures. A further 16-episode comparison evaluates an engineered guard that prioritizes pending notice submissions over local work. It completes 4/4 held-out settings, compared with 1/4 for a calibrated assisted baseline. Each episode contains one large language model actor and two fixed peers. These results establish diagnostic distinctions and bounded policy feasibility under explicit simulation assumptions; they do not establish frontier-model reliability or autonomous team adaptation.
  </details>

- **[Peer Memory Changes Who LLM Agents Consult Without a Detected Gain in Answer Accuracy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09990)**  `arXiv:2611.09990`  
  _Jeffrey Chu, Anjali Joseph, Rivan Mandot, Feker Demere, Vincent Li_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multi-agent LLM systems often reuse the same agents across tasks, creating an opportunity to draw on past interactions when deciding whom to consult. We study this form of memory with PeerMem, which saves MACE's LinUCB state and reuses it when the same agents return. Using six agents, a fixed set of 80 HotpotQA questions, and 12 paired lineages per model, we compare cold, warm, and shuffled initialization in an answer-exchange protocol with reference-answer feedback. Under stable evidence access, warm memory lowers pooled hindsight regret and increases consultation of other evidence holders on Qwen3-32B and Gemma-4-31B-it, while final token F1 differences remain uncertain. Qwen interaction traces further show that warm agents more often encounter peer answers that score above their own prior answers. We extend the evaluation to Qwen3.5-9B using freshly learned memory to compare warm and cold initialization under reassigned and paired stable roles. The primary changed-minus-stable final-F1 interaction is -1.38 points, with a 95% interval of [-3.50,+0.73]. Together, these experiments trace the effects of peer memory through consultation, answer revision, and final task performance.
  </details>

- **[AIM: Adaptive Interaction in Multi-Agent Debate for Multimodal LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08950)**  `arXiv:2611.08950`  
  _Wei Fan, JinYi Yoon, Bo Ji_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) improves reasoning on multimodal tasks, but its accuracy and token efficiency depend on how agents interact during debate. A largely overlooked design choice is which interaction modalities agents use to exchange evidence. Existing methods rely on fixed text- or graph-based interaction, which fails to convey fine-grained multimodal evidence and thus degrades accuracy while inflating token cost due to verbose descriptions. To address this, we propose Adaptive Interaction in Multi-Agent Debate (AIM), an adaptive routing framework that dynamically selects the optimal modality combination for inter-agent interaction in multimodal MAD. Beyond text and graph, AIM introduces task-dependent modality interaction, where agents exchange targeted regions of interest from the task-specific multimodal input, such as image regions, audio segments, or spatio-temporal video clips. To determine the best combination for each instance, AIM first generates a structured baseline response and extracts interpretable routing features that capture which evidence the instance requires, how confident the baseline agent is, and how much new evidence each modality would add beyond the baseline response. A lightweight router then uses these routing features to select a modality combination that avoids both under-fusion (i.e., agents miss decisive evidence) and over-fusion (i.e., redundant modalities inflate token cost) risks. Across eight benchmarks spanning three multimodal task families, AIM achieves the highest accuracy. Combining modalities improves accuracy by up to 6.4% over the best single-modality baseline, and adapting the combination per instance adds up to 4.2% over the most accurate fixed combination of each benchmark with up to 53.4% fewer tokens.
  </details>

- **[MAC-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Collaboration via Interconnected Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01728)**  `arXiv:2611.01728`  
  _Zerui Chen, Qinggang Zhang, Qichuan Liu, Zhishang Xiang, Zhimin Wei, Yunbo Tang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) tackle challenging tasks by dividing work among agents and coordinating their contributions toward shared objectives. Evaluating these systems therefore requires benchmarks that assess not only task-solving performance but also the ability to handle interdependent work. However, existing benchmarks often emphasize task difficulty without substantial collaboration requirements or evaluate only a limited range of predefined collaboration patterns. In this paper, we introduce MAC-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaboration through interconnected tasks. Rather than imposing predefined agent roles or communication protocols, MAC-Bench embeds collaboration requirements directly into task dependencies and shared-resource constraints. Specifically, we mine reusable collaboration structures from selected benchmark tasks at two levels. Local collaboration patterns capture recurring interactions among subtasks, while global task structures characterize how these interactions contribute to complete workflows. Through coarse-to-fine composition, these structures are recombined into task graphs combining different collaboration requirements. Tasks are instantiated in executable environments with automated verification of partial progress and complete task resolution.
  </details>

- **[When Disclosure Is Compulsory: Evaluating Ride-Hailing Rebalancing Policies with Self-Interested LLM Driver Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.41132)**  `arXiv:2610.41132`  
  _Xinyu Wang, Andres Fielbaum_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The EU Platform Work Directive, to be transposed by December 2026, requires ride-hailing platforms to state in plain language the main parameters of their automated decisions and how a worker's behaviour affects them. Such rules are exactly what a large language model (LLM) can read, so drivers will be able to let one decide for them. We compare two main families of rebalancing policy once their rules are public: a reactive policy (R) that sends idle drivers to cover requests just lost, and an anticipatory policy (A) that plans moves on a demand forecast. Each driver is an LLM agent maximizing its own net income, given no rules (N) or the rules at the directive's level of detail (L). We test two LLMs, Claude Haiku 5.5 and Jev, which understand the rules equally well, in a three-zone model and in Manhattan. With the rules disclosed, drivers follow the platform more closely: in Manhattan, the share of relocation offers they decline falls from about four in five to one in four under both policies. Yet the effects differ by policy. For the platform, disclosure costs R 3.7% of its profit in Manhattan, as R now pays for moves drivers used to make for free, while A's profit is unchanged; the two policies, which tie on profit under full compliance, end 6.1% apart. For drivers, disclosure raises income in the small model under both policies and LLMs; for users, it raises the service rate there by 10 to 18 percentage points. In Manhattan, self-interested drivers also make A a win-win-win against full compliance, raising driver income, platform profit and service rate by 10 to 12% each. Rebalancing policies that perform equally well under full compliance can thus show opposite results under mandatory disclosure. The study offers a framework to evaluate such policies under the new requirement and is, to our knowledge, the first to do so with LLM agents.
  </details>

- **[FlowMAS: Learning Multi-Agent Workflow Topology via Information-guided Generative Flow Network](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37151)**  `arXiv:2609.37151`  
  _Haitao Wang, Chenjing Liang, Haipeng Zhang, Jiawei Hu, Sicheng Wang, Songzhu Mei, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Automated multi-agent systems offer clear advantages over manually designed ones in scalability and adaptability, but existing workflow topology methods still face important limitations. Search-based methods are often computationally expensive, textual-gradient-based methods rely on coarse-grained feedback, and existing generation-based methods are not well suited to discrete workflow topologies with complex dependencies. To address these limitations, we propose FlowMAS, a multi-agent workflow topology method based on Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets). FlowMAS models workflow generation as reward-guided flow over the topology space and introduces three components: a GFlowNet-based topology generation backbone, a curiosity-driven module for structure-aware exploration, and an information-guided optimization module for evaluating intermediate topologies. Concretely, the curiosity-driven module encourages exploration of structurally novel workflows, while the information-guided module measures both the information contribution and the communication efficiency of different operators to favor more informative and effective collaboration patterns. Experiments on six benchmark datasets with three LLM backbones show that FlowMAS consistently outperforms multiple baselines.
  </details>

- **[Rate-Aware Quantum-Inspired Trajectory Learning for Interference-Limited Multi-UAV Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25480)**  `arXiv:2606.25480`  
  _Khaoula Khaled, Muhammad Afaq, Zeeshan Kaleem_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Placing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) as aerial base stations is non-convex and combinatorial, so practical methods first discretize the continuous airspace into a finite set of candidate positions---a uniform grid or clustering centroids---and optimize over that set. Built from Euclidean distance alone, the candidate set is channel-blind: it ignores line-of-sight probability and the co-channel interference that limits achievable rate under full frequency reuse. No optimizer can select a position the candidate set omits, so good locations the geometry missed are lost before the search begins. We propose Rate-Aware Quantum-Assisted Graph Condensation (RA-QAGC), a two-stage framework that makes the candidate set itself the object of optimization. The first stage constructs it by annealing a cost that embeds tier-weighted achievable rate, mean co-channel interference, and an explicit minimum-rate penalty, yielding a compact, mobility-feasible waypoint graph. The second stage learns trajectories over that graph with decentralized independent Q-learning agents, replacing a centralized joint-action table with one compact table per UAV. RA-QAGC improves priority-tier throughput by 21--54\% over seven baselines, including recent graph-neural and deep Q-network schemes, at no significant cost in aggregate throughput, and the margin widens as the fleet densifies. We additionally examine the quantum-inspired acceptance rule that recent aerial-networking work advocates, and report that its tunnelling floor confers no measurable advantage over classical simulated annealing at any fleet size tested, while annealing itself clearly outperforms greedy and random placement.
  </details>

- **[LAMaS: A Modular Platform for Learning Low-Latency Multi-Agent Orchestration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10560)**  `arXiv:2601.10560`  
  _Xi Shi, Mengxin Zheng, Qian Lou_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In a multi-agent system (MAS), removing an expensive agent call can save tokens without making the answer arrive sooner: latency depends on the longest chain of dependent calls. We present Latency-Aware Multi-agent System (LAMaS), a modular platform for learning low-latency orchestration. A framework can send a query to LAMaS and receive an answer and execution trace, or keep its own graph builder and use the platform's latency-optimized orchestration layer. During training, the layer gives operators on the critical path the greatest latency penalty while targeting a floor on expected accuracy. During inference, a lightweight controller uses partial results to decide whether to skip work that has yet to start. Across four benchmarks, LAMaS reduces end-to-end latency by over 50% relative to the evaluated learning-based MAS baselines while maintaining competitive or better accuracy. GDesigner and AgentDropout retain their graph builders and train the controller on their own traces; both achieve lower latency across the same benchmarks.
  </details>

- **[Simulating Vein Compressibility for Ultrasound-Guided Femoral Access: Speed, Accuracy, and Phantom Validation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12818)**  `arXiv:2611.12818`  
  _Amit Manicka, Laurent Coulon, Darwin Ang, Michael Loushin, Timothy M. Kowalewski_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  In ultrasound-guided femoral access, probe pressure deforms the tissue and changes the vascular anatomy a robot observes. A simulator must reproduce these mechanics fast enough for robotic interaction, yet the computational effort needed for a clinically meaningful signal like vein collapse before artery is unclear. We test the feasibility of a physics-based simulation in NVIDIA's Isaac Sim for Healthcare, with Stable Neo-Hookean tissue solved by Vertex Block Descent on one GPU. A simulation of a low-fidelity cylindrical benchtop phantom with known geometry and mechanical properties, pressed by a robot, predicted its artery within 5 percentage points at every depth. It matched the vein within 3 points through 11 mm of a 25.4 mm press and followed the collapse behavior of the low-fidelity physical phantom. Across element size, time step, and solver iterations, wall clock time per frame scaled linearly with solver work, but accuracy did not improve with more work. The chosen setting reduced solver time per frame by a factor of 976, from 29,700 ms to 30.4 ms, while remaining within 1.03 points of the finest reference setting. The physics solver alone took 30.4 ms per frame, while the full stack, including ultrasound and graphics rendering, took 56.4 ms per frame. Finally, when seeded with realistic literature-based mechanical properties, the digital leg model compressed the vein far more than the artery at every setting, reproducing the expected clinical signal of vein collapse before artery, which is used to distinguish them. In total, these results suggest that the NVIDIA Isaac Sim platform may be suitable for augmenting reinforcement learning training or online simulation for autonomous femoral access with ultrasound.
  </details>

- **[Learning Heterogeneous Tactile Representation for General Dexterous Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12806)**  `arXiv:2611.12806`  
  _Bing Han, Yichuan Peng, Haoyu Dong, Yuanmeng Hu, Yongyi Jia, Fangjing Wang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Tactile sensing is an indispensable modality for contact-rich dexterous manipulation, a capability that hints at the ultimate frontiers of embodied intelligence. However, commercially available tactile sensors are still at a relatively early stage of development, with each type of sensor offering irreplaceable strengths alongside its own drawbacks. A key challenge is thus to free tactile understanding from sensor-specific physics, so that embodied models can effectively leverage heterogeneous tactile data. To this end, we develop LingBot-Touch, a tactile foundation model characterized by the following properties. (i) Our model yields a unified representation across different tactile sensors (i.e., piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensors), and is easily extensible to new sensor types. (ii) The resulting tactile tokens are plug-and-play: they can be seamlessly integrated into policy models across paradigms, from diffusion policy to vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $\pi_{0.5}$ and LingBot-VLA, consistently enhancing manipulation dexterity. (iii) Extensive experiments, spanning simulation and real-robot deployments across multiple hardware platforms, demonstrate that our tactile representation substantially benefits complex manipulation tasks while maintaining strong computational efficiency. We believe the findings in this work demonstrate the potential of leveraging cross-sensor data to scale tactile learning, and offer encouraging insights for the design of future hardware and embodied models.
  </details>

- **[Benchmarking Real-World Robotic Manipulation through Stochastic Challenges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12804)**  `arXiv:2611.12804`  
  _Elias Gläßer, Gülhan Şikaroğlu, Pavlo Kupyn, Marc Pollefeys, Zuria Bauer, Hermann Blum_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A challenging bottleneck in manipulation research is reproducibility and comparability of methods in real-world environments. Since manipulation is an interactive task, it cannot be evaluated on a static dataset of observations. Benchmarking in simulation is a common remedy, but cannot cover the whole complexity of real-world tests. This paper proposes a new paradigm of stochastic challenges. Like the well-known YCB objects, it is based on reproducible real-world scenes and therefore allows system-level innovation and comparability between different platforms. Due to their stochastic nature, our challenges however, mimic the rigor and surprise of hidden test sets. To this end, we show how different robots in different labs can be compared based on their success rate over different random task samples, if these samples come from the same distribution. We propose stochastic challenges as a general paradigm for robot benchmarking and implement this paradigm in a novel benchmark for mobile manipulation, on which we compare two robots tested in two different labs.
  </details>

- **[Library of Hands: Fix the Hands, Not the World Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12678)**  `arXiv:2611.12678`  
  _Hasaan Ahmad, Qizhen Ying, Yuxuan Sun, Tianjin Huang, Guangming Wang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  A world model predicts how a scene changes after an action, and a planner uses it to search for actions that reach a goal. If the camera moves or the controller changes, the same command moves the robot differently: when its commands are turned by 90 degrees, a frozen planner with the LeWM world model that succeeds in 77.5% of episodes succeeds in only 7.8%.
